name: Central Saanich

facts.text: Under Central Saanich's Tree Management Bylaw (adopted June 2021), removing a tree more than 30 cm in diameter at breast height needs a permit. To get the diameter, divide the circumference by 3.14.
facts.excerpt: trees greater than 30 cm (12") diameter at breast height

facts.text: Central Saanich also protects arbutus, Pacific dogwood, Pacific yew and Garry oak as species, and its older tree page adds shore pine and nesting trees.
facts.excerpt: Arbutus, Pacific Dogwood, Pacific Yew, Garry Oak
facts.note: from search snippet (official site could not be fetched from this session: host blocked)

facts.text: When a protected tree is removed in Central Saanich, the 2021 bylaw requires up to three replacement trees.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Management Bylaw adopted June 29, 2021 (Let's Talk Central Saanich)
facts.excerpt: when a protected tree is removed it is replaced with up to three trees
facts.note: from search snippet (official site could not be fetched from this session: host blocked)

facts.text: Central Saanich has a mapped Erosion District where removing a tree needs an Engineering permit, with a site plan and a geotechnical engineer's report. The District says this can mean two permits, one from Planning and one from Engineering.
facts.sourceTitle: Trees on private property | District of Central Saanich
facts.excerpt: a site plan locating all buildings, structures and trees as well as a geotechnical engineer's report
facts.note: from search snippet (official site could not be fetched from this session: host blocked)

facts.text: Central Saanich charges $75 plus $25 per tree (up to $200) to remove non-hazardous trees, and nothing for a hazardous tree with no development application. The bylaw allows emergency removal of a high-hazard tree before a permit.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree permit application (District of Central Saanich)
facts.excerpt: allows for EMERGENCY removal of a high hazard tree BEFORE obtaining a permit
facts.note: from search snippet (official site could not be fetched from this session: host blocked); fee figures came from the bylaw page snippet, so confirm them

facts.text: Central Saanich is mostly farmland: 61% of its land is in the Agricultural Land Reserve and 18% is inside the Urban Containment Boundary. Many properties border working fields around Saanichton and Island View.
facts.sourceTitle: Central Saanich Today | District of Central Saanich
facts.note: from search snippet (official site could not be fetched from this session: host blocked); excerpt is the figure only, and the place names are our framing

facts.text: Central Saanich sits over named groundwater aquifers, including the Hagan aquifer at Saanichton and the Keating aquifer. Peninsula aquifers are a significant irrigation source for farms.
facts.sourceTitle: Aquifers of the Capital Regional District (BC Water Protection & Sustainability Branch)
facts.excerpt: aquifers on the Saanich Peninsula are also significant sources of water for agricultural irrigation
facts.note: from search snippet (official site could not be fetched from this session: host blocked)

facts.text: Deer damage to crops is a known issue in Central Saanich. It hosted the CRD's rural deer-management pilot from 2013, which included crop-damage inspections on local farms.
facts.sourceTitle: Stay out of the deer control business, staff advise CRD (Times Colonist)
facts.excerpt: one in Central Saanich and one in Oak Bay
facts.note: secondary source; from search snippet; news report, older

facts.text: Regional (CRD, not municipal): from May 1 to September 30, lawns on the regional water supply may be watered two days a week by address (even: Wednesday and Saturday; odd: Thursday and Sunday). The day limits apply only to lawns.
facts.excerpt: The watering schedule days only apply to lawns!
